Jesus and Israel: One Covenant or Two?
Argues that Jesus fulfils Israel's identity, land, temple and law, so that God's promises to Israel are kept in Christ, while also discussing the place of the Jewish people in Romans 11.
The Promise of the Future
A Reformed amillennial survey of eschatology, including chapters on the future of Israel, the millennium and the new creation.
The Gospel and the Land: Early Christianity and Jewish Territorial Doctrine
A major historical study of how the New Testament writers treated the land promise, concluding that they largely transferred holy-space concerns to the person of Christ.
Whose Land? Whose Promise? What Christians Are Not Being Told about Israel and the Palestinians
Examines the biblical land promises and their application in the New Testament, and criticises Christian Zionist readings of the modern conflict, with attention to Palestinian Christians.
Bound for the Promised Land: The Land Promise in God's Redemptive Plan
A volume in the New Studies in Biblical Theology series tracing the land promise from Eden through Canaan to the new creation in Christ.
Romans (Baker Exegetical Commentary on the New Testament)
A detailed exegetical commentary on Romans which argues that Romans 11:26 foresees a future large-scale salvation of ethnic Jews through faith in Christ.
Future Israel: Why Christian Anti-Judaism Must Be Challenged
A premillennial, Calvinistic defence of a continuing future for ethnic and national Israel, critical of supersessionist readings in church history.
Israelology: The Missing Link in Systematic Theology
A Messianic Jewish dispensational systematic study of Israel past, present and future, arguing for a permanent distinction between Israel and the church.
The Promise-Plan of God: A Biblical Theology of the Old and New Testaments
Traces one unified promise-plan through Scripture and argues that the promises to Israel, including the land, remain part of that plan.
The New Christian Zionism: Fresh Perspectives on Israel and the Land
Essays by several scholars arguing for a continuing theological significance of the Jewish people and the land without depending on a full dispensational system.
In Defense of Israel
A popular case by the founder of Christians United for Israel for Christian support of the Jewish people and the State of Israel on biblical grounds.
Christian Zionism: Road-map to Armageddon?
A critical history and theological assessment of Christian Zionism from its nineteenth-century roots to its modern political influence.
The Davidic Promise and the Inclusion of the Gentiles (Amos 9:9-15 and Acts 15:13-18): A Test Passage for Theological Systems
Journal of the Evangelical Theological Society 20/2. Kaiser argues James sees the Gentile mission as part of the rebuilding of David's house, while the promise to Israel still stands.
James and the Gentiles (Acts 15.13-21)

Essay in History, Literature and Society in the Book of Acts, ed. Ben Witherington III. Bauckham argues James reads the rebuilt tent of David as the eschatological temple, the community of Jews and Gentiles.
A dispensational exposition of the Abrahamic, Davidic and new covenants, arguing for Israel's future national regathering and kingdom.
An Old Testament Theology: An Exegetical, Canonical, and Thematic Approach
A major Old Testament theology. Its chapters on the land argue that the New Testament redefines the land promise in Christ, as heavenly and finally the renewed earth.
Sealed with an Oath: Covenant in God's Unfolding Purpose
New Studies in Biblical Theology 23. A survey of the biblical covenants, including the Abrahamic oath and its national and international strands.
On the Reliability of the Old Testament
An Egyptologist's survey of archaeological and textual evidence for the Old Testament periods, from the patriarchs to the exile and return.
The Tel Dan Stele (Aramaic inscription naming 'the house of David')
9th century BC
Fragments found at Tel Dan in 1993 and 1994, now in the Israel Museum. The earliest known extra-biblical reference to David's dynasty (bytdwd).
The Cyrus Cylinder
c. 539 BC
A clay cylinder found at Babylon in 1879, now in the British Museum. It records Cyrus's conquest of Babylon and his policy of returning displaced peoples and their gods to their homes.
Assyrian and Babylonian Chronicles
A standard edition of the Mesopotamian chronicles, including the Babylonian Chronicle (ABC 5) that dates Nebuchadnezzar's capture of Jerusalem to 2 Adar 597 BC.
The Coming Prince
Classic calculation of Daniel's seventy weeks using 360-day prophetic years from Artaxerxes' decree to Nehemiah, ending at the triumphal entry, with the seventieth week placed in the future.
Jesus and the Land: The New Testament Challenge to 'Holy Land' Theology
Argues that the New Testament relocates the holiness of the land to Jesus himself and widens the inheritance to the world, challenging theologies that make the modern territory theologically central.
Der Judenstaat (The Jewish State)
Herzl's founding pamphlet of political Zionism, arguing that antisemitism made a Jewish state, secured by international agreement, a practical necessity.
The Balfour Declaration (letter to Lord Rothschild, 2 November 1917)
British government statement favouring a national home for the Jewish people in Palestine, with a proviso protecting the civil and religious rights of existing non-Jewish communities.
United Nations General Assembly Resolution 181 (II): Future Government of Palestine
The partition plan recommending separate Jewish and Arab states and an international regime for Jerusalem, adopted 29 November 1947 by 33 votes to 13 with 10 abstentions.
Declaration of the Establishment of the State of Israel
The founding declaration read by David Ben-Gurion on 14 May 1948, grounding the state in Jewish history, the Balfour Declaration, the Holocaust and the UN resolution.
The Origins of Christian Zionism: Lord Shaftesbury and Evangelical Support for a Jewish Homeland
A historian's study of British evangelical restorationism, centred on Shaftesbury, and its role in the background to Zionism.
1948: A History of the First Arab-Israeli War
A detailed military and political history of the 1947-49 war, including the causes of the Palestinian refugee exodus.
Israel: A History
A general history of Zionism and the State of Israel from the 1880s to the early twenty-first century.
A History of Zionism
A standard history of the Zionist movement from its nineteenth-century roots to the founding of the state.
Messianism, Zionism, and Jewish Religious Radicalism
Analyses the range of Orthodox Jewish responses to Zionism, from Haredi opposition (including Satmar) to Rabbi Kook's religious Zionism.
Vayoel Moshe
A Hebrew treatise arguing from Jewish law and tradition that establishing a Jewish state before the coming of the Messiah is forbidden.
"A Land without a People for a People without a Land"
Middle East Quarterly article tracing the origin and use of the slogan, including its links with Alexander Keith, Shaftesbury and Israel Zangwill.
Apocalypsis Apocalypseos (A Revelation of the Revelation)
An influential Puritan commentary on Revelation that expected the conversion of the Jews and their return to the land.
The Mystery of Israel's Salvation Explained and Applyed
A New England Puritan's case for a future national conversion of the Jews and their restoration.
Jesus Is Coming
A widely circulated premillennial book by the author of the 1891 Blackstone Memorial, teaching Israel's restoration as a sign of the end.
Jerusalem Countdown: A Warning to the World
A popular Christian Zionist book by the founder of Christians United for Israel, reading current Middle East events through prophecy.
A Journal of the Evangelical Theological Society article arguing that Acts 15 confirms the Gentile part of Amos 9 while the national promise remains.
Epicenter: Why the Current Rumblings in the Middle East Will Change Your Future
A popular book reading Ezekiel 38-39 as a coming invasion of Israel by Russia, Iran and allies.
Eye to Eye: Facing the Consequences of Dividing Israel
Argues from Joel 3:2 and Genesis 12:3 that pressure on Israel to divide the land has been followed by disasters.
The Last Word on the Middle East
A Pentecostal Bible teacher's case that Israel's regathering fulfils prophecy and that Christians should support it.
The Politics of Christian Zionism, 1891-1948
A historian's account of Christian Zionist influence on British and American policy from the Blackstone Memorial to 1948.
Evangelicals and Israel: The Story of American Christian Zionism
A study of American Christian Zionism's beliefs, motives and political influence, based on extensive interviews.
Christ and Time: The Primitive Christian Conception of Time and History

Swiss New Testament scholar who argued that the decisive battle of salvation history was won at the cross and resurrection, while the final victory waits for Christ's return; his D-Day and V-Day picture shaped the later 'already / not yet' consensus.
The Teaching of Jesus Concerning the Kingdom of God and the Church

Short study by the Princeton biblical theologian arguing that Jesus taught the kingdom as both present in his ministry and future in its consummation, and that the church is the present form of the kingdom.
The Greatness of the Kingdom: An Inductive Study of the Kingdom of God
Classic dispensational study tracing the mediatorial kingdom from the Old Testament through its offer and postponement in the Gospels to its establishment in the millennium.
Continuity and Discontinuity: Perspectives on the Relationship Between the Old and New Testaments

Essays in honour of S. Lewis Johnson in which covenant and dispensational scholars debate in pairs; it includes Bruce Waltke's essay 'Kingdom Promises as Spiritual' and dispensational essays on the same questions.
The God of Israel and Christian Theology
A study of supersessionism in Christian theology, distinguishing several kinds and proposing a reading of the canon that keeps God's covenant with Israel central.
Toward an Old Testament Theology
Presents the Old Testament as one unfolding promise-plan of God, with the promise of land and nation to Israel as a lasting part of that plan.

Who is Israel in the promises of God? The Old Testament promised Abraham a seed, a land and blessing for the nations (Genesis 12:1-3). It promised David a son on an everlasting throne (2 Samuel 7:12-16), and it promised Jerusalem a glorious temple, a return from exile and a new covenant (Jeremiah 31:31-34). Christians agree that these promises meet in Jesus Christ, 'the Son of David, the son of Abraham' (Matthew 1:1). They disagree about what that means for the Jewish people and for the land. The fulfilment family (covenant amillennialists, postmillennialists, partial preterists and progressive covenantalists) holds that every promise has found its 'Yes' in Christ (2 Corinthians 1:20) and now belongs to all who are in him, Jew and Gentile alike, so that no second, national fulfilment is required. The future family (historic premillennialists in part, progressive and classic dispensationalists, and Christian Zionists) holds that God will still keep his specific promises to ethnic, national Israel, including the land and a kingdom centred on Jerusalem, because 'the gifts and the calling of God are irrevocable' (Romans 11:29). This study traces each promise from its first giving to where the New Testament says it lands. It sets out the history of the modern State of Israel, founded in 1948, and asks whether that state fulfils prophecy. It weighs the present reign of Christ against a future earthly kingdom. Each camp is given in its strongest form, with its best answers. The theological question is kept separate from the dignity of the Jewish people, whom both families are bound to love (Romans 10:1).
Who are the people of God?

If believing Gentiles are 'Abraham's seed, heirs according to the promise' (Galatians 3:29), then the church is the one continuing people of God, rooted in Israel's olive tree (Romans 11:17). If Israel and the church are two peoples with two sets of promises, then the church is a distinct new body, and national Israel still waits for its own inheritance. The answer shapes how believers read their own place in the story of Scripture.
How the two Testaments fit together

The debate is at bottom a debate about method. Does the New Testament explain the true sense of Old Testament promises (Luke 24:27, 44-45), or must every promise be kept in the exact form in which Israel first heard it? Each answer produces a different reading of the prophets, of Revelation 20 and of Romans 11. Readers who settle this question usually settle the rest.
Is Christ reigning now on David's throne?

Peter preached that God raised Jesus to sit on David's throne (Acts 2:30-36). Fulfilment scholars take this to mean the Davidic kingdom is already present, from heaven, and spreads by the gospel. Dispensationalists traditionally place the Davidic reign in a future millennium in Jerusalem; progressive dispensationalists say it has begun now and will be completed on earth later. The question decides whether Christians wait for the kingdom or live already within it.
Prophecy, politics and the Middle East

Since 1948, and especially since the Six-Day War in 1967, many Christians have read the modern State of Israel as fulfilled prophecy and have given it strong political support on that basis (Genesis 12:3). Others, including many Palestinian and Arab Christians, argue that this reading turns a political state into a sacred object and overlooks justice for all peoples in the land. The study separates what Scripture teaches from what any government does, and takes no side on current political or military disputes.
Love for the Jewish people

Paul grieved for his kinsmen and prayed for their salvation (Romans 9:1-5; Romans 10:1). He warned Gentile believers not to boast against the natural branches (Romans 11:18-21) and said that the Jewish people remain 'beloved for the sake of their forefathers' (Romans 11:28). The long history of Christian contempt for Jews, from medieval expulsions to the Holocaust, demands care in this debate. Neither family, at its best, teaches hatred; the question is how God's love for Israel is expressed in Christ.
Covenant amillennialism

Covenant amillennialists read the Bible as one unfolding covenant of grace, from the promise in Genesis 3:15 to the new creation. The promises made to Abraham, Moses and David are not cancelled but fulfilled in Christ, the true Israel, and shared by all who are united to him by faith. The 'thousand years' of Revelation 20 is the present age between Christ's first and second comings, in which Christ reigns and Satan is bound so that the gospel reaches the nations. The hope of the believer is not a restored Jewish kingdom but the new heavens and new earth.

Israel was always defined by promise and faith, not by birth alone: 'not all who are descended from Israel are Israel' (Romans 9:6). Jesus, the obedient Son, embodies Israel (Matthew 2:15), and all who belong to him, believing Jews and Gentiles together, form 'the Israel of God' (Galatians 6:16). The church is not a replacement of Israel but Israel's faithful remnant enlarged by the grafting in of Gentiles (Romans 11:17-24).

The land of Canaan was a real gift and a type. Abraham himself looked for a heavenly country and a city with foundations (Hebrews 11:10, 16), and Paul says the promise was that he would inherit 'the world' (Romans 4:13). The land promise widens in Christ to the whole renewed earth, which the meek will inherit (Matthew 5:5).

The kingdom of God came with Christ, is present now as he reigns from heaven at the right hand of God (Ephesians 1:20-22), and will be revealed in fullness at his single return. There is no future earthly millennium; the next great event is the return of Christ, the general resurrection and the judgment.

The modern state is not seen as a fulfilment of prophecy. It is a political entity, founded by a largely secular Zionist movement in 1948 and judged like any other nation. Its people are loved and evangelised like all others, and many amillennialists take care to reject antisemitism.

Views differ. Calvin read 'all Israel' as the whole church of Jews and Gentiles. Bavinck, Hoekema, Robertson and Hendriksen read it as the full number of elect Jews saved through the whole age. Some amillennialists, such as Kim Riddlebarger, expect a future large-scale turning of Jews to Christ before his return, without any national kingdom.

Postmillennialists share covenant theology's reading of the promises but are optimistic about history. Christ reigns now from heaven, and through the preaching of the gospel and the work of the Spirit most of the world's peoples will be converted before he returns (Psalms 2:8; Matthew 28:18-20). The millennium is the long era of gospel triumph that comes before the second coming. Many postmillennialists, following the Puritans, expect the conversion of the Jewish people to be part of that triumph.

The church of Jew and Gentile is the one people of God and the heir of Israel's promises. Yet ethnic Jews keep a special place in God's providence: their future conversion will bring 'life from the dead' for the world (Romans 11:15). This is a conversion into the one church, not the creation of a separate national people.

The land promise is fulfilled in Christ and extends to the whole earth, which will be filled with the knowledge of the Lord as the waters cover the sea (Isaiah 11:9; Habakkuk 2:14). Some older postmillennialists, such as some Puritans, did expect Jews to return to Palestine, but this was not central to the system.

Christ's Davidic kingdom is already reigning and will grow like a mustard seed until it fills the earth (Matthew 13:31-33). There is no future earthly kingdom after Christ returns; his return closes history with resurrection and judgment.

Most modern postmillennialists see the State of Israel as a secular political state with no prophetic standing. They hope for Jewish people to come to Christ, not for the state's expansion. Some note that earlier Puritan hopes were for the conversion of the Jews, not for a state founded without faith in Christ.

Most expect a future large-scale conversion of ethnic Jews within the church, leading to wider blessing for the nations. This is the 'Puritan hope' traced by Iain Murray. A minority read 'all Israel' as the whole elect church.

Partial preterists hold that many prophecies which others place in the future were fulfilled in the first century, above all in the destruction of Jerusalem and the temple by Rome in AD 70 (Matthew 24:34). Jesus warned that the kingdom would be taken from the leaders of Israel and given to a people producing its fruit (Matthew 21:43), and that judgment would fall on 'this generation' (Matthew 23:36). AD 70 marked the end of the old covenant order and showed that the new covenant people in Christ is God's temple. Partial preterists still hold to Christ's future bodily return, the resurrection and the final judgment, which separates them from full preterism, a view outside the historic creeds.

The true Israel is the Messiah and the remnant who believed in him, joined by the Gentiles. Old covenant Israel as a national, temple-centred institution came to its appointed end in AD 70. Ethnic Jews remain loved and are called to the same faith as all others.

The land, temple and Jerusalem served their purpose as shadows until the coming of Christ (Hebrews 8:13). The heavenly Jerusalem is now 'our mother' (Galatians 4:26), and believers have come to Mount Zion (Hebrews 12:22).

The kingdom came with power in the generation of the apostles (Mark 9:1) and is now advancing. Most partial preterists are postmillennial, a few are amillennial. None expect a future earthly Jewish kingdom.

The modern state has no prophetic link to texts that, on this view, were fulfilled by AD 70. Preterists criticise 'newspaper exegesis' and the many failed predictions tied to 1948 and 1967. Some debate whether 'until the times of the Gentiles are fulfilled' (Luke 21:24) hints at a later change for Jerusalem; this is disputed among them.
Opinions vary. Many partial preterists, following the Puritans, expect a future conversion of Jews to Christ; others read 'all Israel' as the whole people of God.

Progressive covenantalism, set out by Peter Gentry and Stephen Wellum in Kingdom through Covenant (2012), reads the Bible as a series of covenants (Noah, Abraham, Israel, David) that progressively unfold and are all fulfilled in the new covenant in Christ. It agrees with dispensationalists that the new covenant is truly new, and with covenant theologians that Israel's promises are fulfilled in Christ. The key move is typology: Israel, the land and the temple are real historical types whose antitype is Christ and, through him, his people.

Christ is the true Israel, the obedient Son and Servant (Isaiah 49:3). The church is not simply 'the new Israel' by direct transfer, but it receives Israel's promises because it is united to Christ, Israel's antitype. Ethnic Jews who believe are part of this one new man (Ephesians 2:15).

The land is a type of the new creation. Oren Martin in Bound for the Promised Land (2015) traces how the land promise, already pointing back to Eden, widens to the whole renewed world (Romans 4:13; Revelation 21:1-3). A restoration of Canaan alone would be a step back from the fulfilment.

The kingdom was inaugurated by Christ's death, resurrection and enthronement and will be consummated at his return. Most progressive covenantalists are amillennial, though some are historic premillennial; the system does not require one view of Revelation 20.
The 1948 state is not regarded as a fulfilment of prophecy, since the promises run through Christ, not apart from him. Proponents usually stress love and evangelism toward Jewish people.
Thomas Schreiner and others hold that Romans 11:26 promises a future large-scale salvation of ethnic Jews through faith in Christ. This conversion does not bring a separate national kingdom.

Historic premillennialists, following early writers such as Justin Martyr and Irenaeus, expect Christ to return before an earthly reign of a thousand years (Revelation 20:4-6). Unlike dispensationalists, most do not hold a strict distinction between Israel and the church, and they agree that the church shares in Israel's promises now. George Eldon Ladd argued that the New Testament reinterprets Old Testament prophecy around Christ. Yet many in this camp still expect a future turning of ethnic Israel to Christ, linked to his return.

The church is the people of God and the spiritual Israel, but ethnic Israel has not lost its place in God's purposes. Ladd held that 'all Israel' in Romans 11:26 means a future salvation of literal Israel, within the one people of God. Some, like Barry Horner, argue strongly for a continuing national identity.

Views vary. Ladd tended to read the land promises through Christ. Others in this camp, such as Barry Horner and earlier writers like J. C. Ryle and C. H. Spurgeon, expected the Jews to be restored to their land.

The kingdom is 'already and not yet': it came in Christ's ministry and is present in power (Matthew 12:28), but it will appear on earth in an intermediate millennial reign after Christ returns, before the eternal state.
Views vary widely. Some see the modern state as a providential event that may prepare for Israel's future turning to Christ; others, like Ladd, refused to tie prophecy to any political state.
Most expect a future large-scale conversion of ethnic Jews at or just before Christ's return (Romans 11:25-27; Zechariah 12:10). This conversion opens the millennial blessing.

Progressive dispensationalism arose in the 1980s and 1990s through Craig Blaising, Darrell Bock and Robert Saucy. It agrees that Christ already reigns on David's throne from heaven (Acts 2:30-36) and that the church shares in the new covenant now. But it insists that the kingdom will be completed on earth, with a restored and saved national Israel in its land among the redeemed nations. Its model is 'already and not yet': the Davidic promises are inaugurated now and consummated in the millennium and new creation.

Israel means ethnic, national Israel, and the church is a multi-ethnic people that includes Jews and Gentiles. Gentiles share in Israel's spiritual blessings without becoming Israel, just as the nations in the prophets are blessed alongside Israel (Isaiah 19:24-25). Michael Vlach stresses that nations remain nations in the new creation (Revelation 21:24-26).

The land promise to Abraham's physical descendants remains in force (Genesis 17:8). It will be fulfilled when Christ returns and Israel, saved and restored, lives securely in its land within a renewed earth that also includes the nations.

Jesus now reigns on David's throne in heaven, but the kingdom will come on earth in a future millennium, with Jerusalem as a centre, followed by the eternal state. The apostles' question about restoring the kingdom to Israel was about timing, not about whether it would happen (Acts 1:6-7).

Most progressive dispensationalists are cautious. They distinguish the secular state from the future restoration of Israel in faith (Ezekiel 36:24-28), while allowing that God may be preparing the way. They urge justice for all peoples in the land.
Romans 11:26 promises a future national salvation of ethnic Israel when the Deliverer comes from Zion (Romans 11:26-27). This salvation leads to national restoration in the land.

Classic dispensationalism, shaped by John Nelson Darby in the 1830s and spread by the Scofield Reference Bible (1909), reads history as a series of dispensations. It holds that God has two distinct peoples: Israel, with earthly promises, and the church, with heavenly ones. The church age is a 'parenthesis' or 'intercalation' not seen by the Old Testament prophets. After the rapture of the church, God will resume his program with Israel in the seventieth week of Daniel (Daniel 9:24-27) and then fulfil the land and throne promises literally in a thousand-year kingdom.

Israel always means the physical descendants of Jacob. Charles Ryrie named a consistent distinction between Israel and the church as the essential mark of dispensationalism, alongside literal interpretation and the glory of God as the unifying theme. Galatians 6:16 refers to believing Jews, not to the whole church.
